To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the decision to test urine gram stain at the initial visit of lower urinary tract infection depends on the prevalence of gram negative rods in the population and the treatment efficacy of antibiotics.

the initial testing of gram-stained smear of urine for selection of effective antibiotics on women with acute urinary tract infections is cost effective when the prevalence of gram positive cocci infection is high or when the efficacy of the antibiotics therapy is low.
the gram stain test is cost effective when the pretest probability of gram negative rods is higher than 0.90.

the decision analysis model for the initial treatment strategy of women with lower urinary infection.
the clinical and economic aspects of the routine urine gram stain testing on women with acute uncomplicated dysuria.
the clinical and economic aspects of the initial testing of gram stained smears for selecting antibiotics on women with acute lower urinary tract infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the gram stain strategy was cost effective for the initial visit on patients with acute dysuria if the frequency of gram negative rods infection would be increased, and the treatment efficacy after the initial antibiotics therapy would be reduced.
the decision of doing or not doing urine gram stain for selecting antibiotics at initial visits on women with dysuria should be based on the local situation.

the gram stain test for the selection of antibiotics at the initial visits on women with acute urinary tract infections should be done only in cases where the prevalence of gram negative rods is high.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the routine urine gram stain testing was not always cost effective for selecting antibiotics on women with acute lower urinary tract infection.

the routine urine gram stain testing was not cost effective for women with acute dysuric symptoms, unless there was a high pretest probability of gram negative infection or there was a high frequency of resistant pathogens.
the gram stain test is useful when the frequency of the gram positive coccus infections would be increased or if we could not expect the high efficacy of the antibiotic therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the gram stain test is useful for selecting antibiotics when the prevalence of pathogens to be the gram negative rods is 90% or more, and the test is not cost effective when the prevalence of gram positive coccic infection is high.
the decision to do or not do gram stain test for the selection of antibiotics at initial visit on women who have acute dysuria is a trade-off between the direct costs and expected days of treatment.
it is important for physicians to consider the cost-effectiveness of the laboratory test in selecting antibiotics for women with acute dysuriac.
